title: How Moss Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how moss works: its origins during the Ordovician period and its role in triggering ice ages by drawing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere through rock-leaching; moss anatomy (gametophyte, sporophyte, capsule, operculum, rhizoids instead of roots); water uptake by capillary action; photosynthesis; sexual reproduction via archegonia and antheridia and spore dispersal, plus asexual fragmentation; moss diversity (about 15,000 species, granite, peat/sphagnum and true mosses); dormancy; growing moss with buttermilk and shade; removing moss from roofs and lawns; and using moss to find north. The episode closes with a listener mail from John Keating in Dublin about fraternities, and a call for listener moss stories.

segments.title: Opening banter and cheeks
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about Chuck's cheek poll, a made-up moss joke, and windy weather before introducing the topic.

segments.title: Moss and the start of ice ages
segments.summary: Josh describes the Ordovician period, when the first bryophytes, including granite mosses, leached minerals from rocks, drew carbon dioxide from the air, cooled the planet by about eight degrees centigrade, and triggered ice ages.

segments.title: Moss overview and types
segments.summary: The hosts note moss has roughly 15,000 species and no true roots, seeds or internal water-moving systems. They cover three groups: granite mosses, peat mosses (sphagnum, used as soil conditioner and fuel), and true mosses. They also discuss moss in extreme places, slow growth under Arctic lake ice, and dormancy that can last years.

segments.title: Moss anatomy
segments.summary: The hosts describe the gametophyte with its leaves and rhizoids, which anchor the plant but do not function as roots. They describe the sporophyte stalk, the capsule, and the operculum.

segments.title: Water uptake, photosynthesis and nutrients
segments.summary: Moss absorbs water through its leaves and through capillary action in its rhizoids, comparing this to a paper towel. The hosts explain photosynthesis, oxygen release, and using sugar to break down minerals.

segments.title: Moss reproduction
segments.summary: Sexual reproduction uses archegonia that produce eggs and antheridia that produce swimming sperm that need moisture to fertilize. The sporophyte releases spores. Moss can also reproduce asexually when fragments break off and root.

segments.title: Growing, caring for and killing moss
segments.summary: Advice on transplanting moss into shade, propagating it by blending it with buttermilk, and feeding and cleaning it. The hosts then discuss removing moss from sidewalks and roofs, using white vinegar or scraping it, and noting that moss on roofs traps moisture and loosens shingles.

segments.title: Finding north with moss
segments.summary: Moss tends to grow on the side of trees with the least sunlight, which is north, a tip for navigating while lost in the woods.

segments.title: Listener mail: John Keating on fraternities
segments.summary: John Keating from Dublin writes about Trinity College's new fraternity, Irish societies versus US frats, and asks why the frat system did not spread outside the US. The hosts agree to consider a fraternities episode.

segments.title: Call for listener moss stories
segments.summary: The hosts ask listeners to send moss stories by tweet, Facebook, or email.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode with a brief sign-off.
